stories.body:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

T here are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration , Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

His alleged actions had risked national security; his fall from power lasted less than two weeks.

According to early reporting, Trump decided late last week to intervene in Huang’s case, thinking that his restoration as Nvidia’s chief could help rally a sluggish stock market. In an economy that has become increasingly dependent on the success of AI companies, Nvidia , which makes the chips that enable the technology, has come to be seen as something of a load-bearing firm, propping up an AI sector which is increasingly understood to be in an overvaluation bubble that will inevitably pop.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. The reinstatement was reportedly orchestrated by Vance, the vice-president and presumptive 2028 Republican nominee, who drew on his own deep ties to friends, allies and benefactors in Silicon Valley to convey the administration’s strong desire for Huang to return.

It marks a remarkable intervention of the executive branch into the personnel decisions of a private firm.

In public statements, Huang’s allies and boosters have repeatedly emphasized the restored CEO as personally essential to the company, downplaying the national security and chip-smuggling concerns in favor of a portrait of a singular mind.

Huang, they say, is unique and irreplaceable, essential to the functioning of Nvidia and hence of the economy; because of this supposed personal specialness, we’re told, it makes sense if he got to spill secrets to China over pillow talk at the expense of your retirement fund.

But it is striking that this deep belief in the irreplaceable brilliance of one AI CEO is so profoundly at odds with the ethos of the AI industry, which promises to automate away all human judgment and experience and make human beings in general – let along anyone human being in particular – profoundly replaceable, if not completely superfluous.

Maybe this, too, is another way that the rules are different for the rich: the tech executives never meant to say that they themselves would become disposable and interchangeable. That fate was reserved for the lowly, like you and me.

It is just this sort of shocking arrogance and display of elite impunity among the tech sector that has disgusted Americans and shocked their consciences; the deep and emphatic rejection of datacenters that was expressed by voters in the recent midterm elections should be understood, I think, as a proxy for a bigger discontent with the recklessness and greed of the tech oligarchs who impose their whims on the country with life-altering consequences.

It is not clear, either, why the Trump administration, which claims that national security and the US economy rely on the returns of AI companies, would want one of the most important of those companies to be helmed by a man who may have been compromised by China, the nation’s primary adversary and main economic competitor.

The flagrancy of the seeming corruption and incompetence at play, and the evident rage of the American people at both, will hopefully spur Democrats to launch serious and probing investigations into Nvidia, Huang, and their ties to the Trump administration when the party takes control of both houses of Congress in January.

In the meantime, Trump himself has indicated that there’s one reason why he has taken a particular interest in Huang’s case: sex. In a statement to the Times, Trump said that he thought Huang had been treated unfairly because of the sexual nature of his scandal, or what the president called “The Payton Place part” – an evident reference, the Times helpfully explained to its less senior readers, to a 1960s soap opera that featured many sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier,” Trump said, “because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.” Call it a kind of sex-pest solidarity. The president, a habitual adulterer who has been accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women and who paid an adult film star to keep quiet about their alleged affair (all of which he denies), seems to see something of himself in the prolifically and allegedly perhaps treasonably adulterous Jensen Huang. Elite impunity may have extra appeal when it can double as male impunity, too.

As if to emphasize the point, Trump took to Truth social to share an AI-generated image of Jensen Huang, in a pose mimicking a famous photograph of Trump himself rising up in the moments after an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2024. In the original photo, Trump held up a fist in triumph, showing that he had survived the gunman’s shots. In the new version that the president posted on Monday morning, Huang held up a red bra.

stories.title: How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back
stories.summary: Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.

On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.

It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.

“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” said an ally of Huang.

But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.

Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.

Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.

Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people said.

Trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board said it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.

The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a company executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

Allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.

Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.

Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

Their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.

While the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A company “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.

One arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.

Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.

“Everyone who was important in the tech world was beating his door down,” said the person.

“He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.

​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so quickly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

“He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” said one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

Huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

No member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

“The midterm elections showed that the wider public is deeply skeptical about all things AI,” the person said. “The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data center build-out is quite fragile.”

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

“While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions.”

Others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Published 47 minutes ago

Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.

However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.

Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.

Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

Nvidia's shares fall 5% at the open

Nvidia’s shares are dropping at the start of trading in New York, as the rally following the return of Jensen Huang yesterday subsides.

Nvidia has fallen by 5.5% in the first couple of minutes of trading, to $155.87. That erodes a small portion of yesterday’s 32% surge.

The chipmaker’s stock is under pressure amid criticism of Huang’s return from both Republicans and Democrats.

Niall Hearty, partner and regulatory lawyer at legal firm Weightmans, warns that reinstating Huang could backfire:

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. It seems extremely premature amid ongoing investigations by the SEC, Nvidia’s Board, the FBI and the Department of Justice. “It is understandable for a company facing this level of reputational turmoil to want to restore stability as quickly as possible. Huang’s return may have temporarily reassured investors, but a recovery in the share price does not resolve the underlying questions about governance and accountability.

Closing summary

Time to wrap up…

The sell-off in US tech stocks has resumed, as Monday’s relief rally following the reappointment of Jensen Huang to run Nvidia quickly faded.

Shares in Nvidia are down 7.7% at $152.35, wiping out around a third of Monday’s jump.

Anthropic , the frontier AI firm which floated last week, are down 9.75% at $79.08, meaning anyone who took part in its IPO (priced at $83 a share) is facing a loss.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, says:

double quotation mark “The loss of the $83 IPO price is a major development, coming so swiftly after the listing. By comparison it was a month before SpaceX suffered the same fate. Launching a major IPO in the midst of one of the biggest tech selloffs of recent times was never going to be great timing, but there was a growing sense of ‘now or never’. Huang’s return seems to have amplified the instinct to sell, given his love for open source models rather than the paid version, and absent a broader market recovery it seems Anthropic is fated to struggle for now.”

This is pulling the wider US market into the red, with the Nasdaq Composite now down 2%.

That has punctured an early feeling of relief in the markets, where Asia-Pacific bourses generally rallied today .

Stocks are sliding amid a backlash to the decision to reappoint Huang, under pressure from the White House.

Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with president Trump.”

And Bernie Sanders has warned AI firms not to expect a bailout if their investments go wrong.

Huang will make several several appearances on Capitol Hill next week where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill Huang over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China

Our US Politics Live blog is keeping tabs on the latest developments:

The rapid expansion of AI data centre construction could exacerbate the US housing shortage by drawing workers away from homebuilding.

Oxford Economics has estimated that up to 45,000 additional workers would be employed in residential construction across the 10 states with the highest data centre spending had employment trends followed those elsewhere in the country.

Matthew Martin , senior US economist at Oxford Economics , explains:

double quotation mark “Data centre projects appear to be bidding up wages. “As data centre demand shows little sign of slowing, the wider premium may make it harder for homebuilders to compete for workers.”

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On Monday 30 November, join Dan Milmo , Professor Dame Wendy Hall , Stuart J. Russell and Alexandra Birch-Mayne as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only.

Book tickets here or at guardian.live

The S&P 500, the flagship US share index, is down 0.4% in early trading at 7,206 points.

But.. the Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 0.4%. reaching 49,795 points. Twenty three of the 30 stocks on the DJIA are up, while Nvidia (-5.5%) is the top faller.

The tech-focused Nasdaq index has opened lower too – it’s down 1.8% at 23,661 points.

Analog Devices (-15%) are the top faller, followed by chipmaker AMD (-10.1%) and SanDisk Corporation (-9.2%).

Anthropic's shares tumble below IPO price

Oof! Anthropic’s share price has tumbled below the level at which the frontier AI company sold shares to investors last week, in its record-breaking float.

Anthropic’s stock has dropped by 8.3% at the start of trading, to $80.34, below the $83 IPO price.

This may sour demand for AI-linked stocks, warns Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

She explains:

double quotation mark A drop below $83 so quickly after its IPO could also weigh on the future earnings reports of its largest backers. For example, if Anthropic’s share price falls sharply, then Google and Alphabet, which hold just under 30% of the stock, could take a hit to their bottom lines. So far, Alphabet and Amazon are posting relatively small losses on Tuesday, but these could worsen if Anthropic’s share price continues to decline.

Nvidia's shares fall 5% at the open

Nvidia’s shares are dropping at the start of trading in New York, as the rally following the return of Jensen Huang yesterday subsides.

Nvidia has fallen by 5.5% in the first couple of minutes of trading, to $155.87. That erodes a small portion of yesterday’s 32% surge.

The chipmaker’s stock is under pressure amid criticism of Huang’s return from both Republicans and Democrats.

Niall Hearty, partner and regulatory lawyer at legal firm Weightmans, warns that reinstating Huang could backfire:

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. It seems extremely premature amid ongoing investigations by the SEC, Nvidia’s Board, the FBI and the Department of Justice. “It is understandable for a company facing this level of reputational turmoil to want to restore stability as quickly as possible. Huang’s return may have temporarily reassured investors, but a recovery in the share price does not resolve the underlying questions about governance and accountability.

Bernie Sanders: Taxpayers will not bailout Big Tech oligarchs.

Democratic senator Bernie Sanders has warned US tech companies not to expect a bailout if their AI investments turn sour.

Posting on X , Sanders says:

double quotation mark One thing must be made certain: If the AI bubble bursts, taxpayers will not bailout Big Tech Oligarchs. Not tomorrow. Not next year. Not ever. If AI companies fail, Big Tech Oligarchs must bail them out, not taxpayers. Our message to these multi-billionaires is simple: If you take out a loan, pay it back. Don’t come begging to taxpayers to bail you out.

WSJ: US prepares to raise tariffs on China and other countries

Fears of a new US-China trade war are rippling through the markets today too.

The Wall Street Journal are reporting that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, according to people familiar with the plans.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could release the results of a tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations later this week, the WSJ adds…..

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene has warned that UK interest rates need to keep rising, unless there is a “miraculous” breakthough in the Middle East conflict.

Speaking in London today, Greene – one of the more hawkish members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee – warned that the BOE is “a little bit behind the curve now.”

She explained:

double quotation mark “I think it’s appropriate to tighten policy further unless there’s a miraculous turnaround in data or in the war.”

The City money markets indicate there’s an 84% chance that the Bank rises interest rates at its next meeting, in mid-December.

Most stock markets in the Gulf region posted gains today, taking their cue from Wall Street yesterday, and then Asia-Pacific markets overnight.

Saudi Arabia’s ⁠benchmark index gained 0.4%, while Dubai’s main share index rose by 0.8%, ​ Abu Dhabi’s market finished 1% higher, and Qatar posted a 0.75% rise.

Meta launches AI assistant Muse - are you planning to use it?

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on their apps – and the high street.

Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

Muse can be used as an app or directly within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. Meta invites users to give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, so they can talk to it as well as assign it tasks such as sending an email, booking travel or buying festive presents.

Meta says:

double quotation mark “From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you.”

So… we’d like to know if you have plans to try Muse, or if you’re already a user. Let us know here :

Meanwhile in the bond markets, the UK has paid a record high price to sell inflation-linked bonds.

Britain’s Debt Management Office sold £3.75bn of an index-linked gilt which matures in 2049, at a real yield (the return after inflation) of 2.5235%. That, Reuters has calculated, is the highest for a syndicated sale since records began in 2005.

This chart from Deutsche Bank shows how the AI/tech selloff of recent weeks has been was one of the bigger declines of recent years:

But, Deutsche Bank’s Henry Allen points out that there are ‘clear differences’ with the other big risk-off moves of the last decade:

First, there wasn’t a sudden and fundamental reassessment of the growth outlook, like when the pandemic began in 2020, or during the Liberation Day selloff of 2025.

Second, there wasn’t a meaningful data deterioration, or even much deterioration at all, as happened in summer 2024, or in the 2015-16 selloff.

Third, there wasn’t a hawkish repricing like 2022. Admittedly, further rate hikes are priced in, but even more hikes were priced in early October when the S&P 500 and the NASDAQ hit their record highs. So that factor hasn’t changed.

If Nvidia’s shares do indeed drop when trading begins, it will take a slice out of President Trump’s wealth.

Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive .

That’s based on the US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times.

The US dollar, which hit a 19-month high yesterday, has dipped by 0.3% against a basket of currencies.

That weakness is helping the pound – it’s up half a cent at $1.3088, up from a one-year low yesterday.

Elsewhere in the markets, Anthropic is at risk of falling below the level at which it sold shares to investors last week.

The frontier AI company’s stock is down 5.6% in premarket trading at $82.74, which would take it below its IPO price of $83 a share.

Anthropic also missed out on yesterday’s rally, and dipped slightly on Monday.

Duncan Ferris, analyst at Freetrade , says

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang has stolen Anthropic and [co-founder] Dario Amodei’s thunder. The massive 31% comeback rally sparked by his Nvidia homecoming has turned retail investors’ heads more than one of the biggest IPOs of all time.

stories.title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
stories.summary: Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026, 15:12 GMT

Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

Andy Burnham's plan to collaborate with social media creators Published 23 July

More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024 Published 16 September

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Badenoch said she had been "pretty shocked" by the videos coming out of the event, questioning whether they were in good taste.

She said that while Burnham might think he was connecting with young people, many people around the world "will think our country is a joke".

She said: "I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks.

"Vladimir Putin, President Xi and all sorts of other people who are hostile to the UK will see these things, they will get reports of them, and they will see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country."

In a reference to Balegde's video, she said: "I think it is a disgrace that Number 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that's where we receive people like President Zelensky, showing them that they have the support of people in this country, is being degraded in this way."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticised the use of the Downing Street door as "puerile" and "demeaning" but said he wouldn't ban influencers from Number 10.

"I wouldn't let them behave quite the way that it happened," he said.

"It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed."

Responding to questions about Balegde's video, the prime minister's spokesperson said "the content was clearly not acceptable", but added "content creators are responsible for what they choose to post".

Asked repeatedly whether Number 10 had requested for the video be removed, the spokesperson said: "It is right the creator took down that content.

"It's clearly not acceptable and that is reflected by the fact that it has been taken down."

They also defended the decision to invite influencers to Downing Street, saying it was "right that the PM listens to" social media content creators who "reach millions of people who don't get their news from traditional media".

Balegde also gave a speech inside the influencers' event, which was held by Burnham in an attempt to build links with a growing sector of the economy.

A smaller group of creators were asked to arrive early to film videos with the prime minister.

One attendee in this group said they had to run ideas past the prime minister's team for approval.

A government spokesperson said they would not comment on security and whether the footage captured on the government phones was reviewed, but said it was "not abnormal" for attendees of Downing Street to use government phones.

stories.title: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis
stories.summary: "Without this funding, activities would be delayed."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
“Without this funding, activities would be delayed.”

As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government ( PDF ).

The list of so-called “funding anomalies” is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA’s Artemis program for a “higher rate of operations.”

The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA’s Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China’s lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA’s, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there.

Another continuing resolution?

Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1 of this year, but the US Congress and White House have not agreed upon a budget. The government, including NASA, has been operating on a “continuing resolution” since that time. The existing continuing resolution remains in effect until December 11, by which time the parties need to agree to a final budget or another continuing resolution, or else the government will shut down.

Given the broad disagreement in funding priorities, it seems most likely that Congress will settle on another continuing resolution, punting a budget deal into the new year and a new Democratic-led House and Senate. The release of the White House “anomalies” document signals to Congress which priorities the Trump administration wants to see addressed in a new continuing resolution that would be agreed to in the coming weeks, which the president would have to sign.

The budget plus-up for Artemis appears to be a significant win for NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, who arrived at the space agency 11 months ago, after the White House had already put together its “President’s Budget request” for the fiscal year 2027 process. This is the first time he has had a chance to work with the Trump administration on budget priorities, and in doing so has convinced officials that NASA deserves more funding in its race back to the Moon.

As part of the description for the funding, the document indicates that NASA is seeking additional funding for Artemis without stripping away money for existing programs in other areas such as science. “Additional topline is needed to support this effort without jeopardizing other priorities outlined in the National Space Policy,” the White House document states.

Flexibility for Isaacman

The key challenge for NASA in the next two years, as part of its return to the Moon, is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to finalize development of their lunar landers—a key untested piece of the mission plan that carries astronauts down from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, provides a temporary habitat there, and then returns the crew members to lunar orbit. The space agency has been seeking to help both companies work through supply chain and test issues.

NASA has also been working to increase its own in-house technical capabilities to help Axiom Space develop a lunar space suit and assist private companies developing a panoply of smaller landers and lunar hardware to provide power, communications, and other services as part of the agency’s Moon Base initiative. These companies all face serious supply chain issues for key hardware components.

“Language is needed to provide an additional $2 billion to meet the schedule for Artemis acceleration activities to include supply chain acceleration via in-house manufacturing and modernization of NASA’s in-house capabilities in areas such as suits, thrusters, SLS-related hardware, habitats, and safety systems for astronauts,” the White House document states. “Without this funding, activities would be delayed, missing the required operational need date.”

Notably, the document also includes the following language: “NASA needs to build and retain the ability to manufacture complex low-rate components and major assemblies.” This suggests the White House wants NASA to have the infrastructure to manufacture specialized components when commercial suppliers cannot deliver them quickly or reliably.

Importantly, the language in the White House funding request appears deliberately broad, giving Isaacman substantial flexibility to identify the most pressing bottlenecks in the Artemis program and direct resources toward addressing them quickly.

stories.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
stories.summary: Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tech Giants

Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.

For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process.

Earlier this month, IBM said it would no longer support the U.S. immigration status of workers in its consulting division, offering them the option to take a role with the company in another country or exit, according to a Bloomberg report citing a company document.

“IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages,” an IBM spokesperson told Rest of World . “That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting.”

IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people globally. The company does not disclose the geographical split for its workforce, making it hard to ascertain the exact number of workers impacted by this decision. On November 19, the company’s career portal listed 1,278 open roles for the consulting division outside the U.S., including 1,125 in India, 23 in Singapore, and 18 in the U.K. In the U.S., it listed 89 roles.

For employees, relocation does not automatically ensure continued engagement, effective collaboration, or equal access to professional opportunities, Zakaria Laaraj, founder of consultancy Global New Ventures, told Rest of World . It may affect their access to decision-makers, established networks, and career opportunities. “The credibility of such an offer depends on employee tenure, available positions, immigration requirements, and compensation,” Laaraj said.

Discussions on Blind, an anonymous employee forum used by 14 million professionals, suggest relocating may not be realistic for many.

Moving to India, for instance, could mean an approximately 80% pay cut, one IBM employee wrote on Blind.

“Employees get three weeks to decide,” Blind’s CEO Sunguk Moon told Rest of World . “The alternative is three months of severance and a last day of December 31. And the news came in a surprise one-on-one ‘career sync’ with a manager.”

For any relocation option to be viable, companies must go beyond just assigning a new job to their employee, George Carrillo, CEO of career development and staffing company HireMe, told Rest of World .

Moving a position can mean uprooting a family.” George Carrillo, CEO of and staffing company HireMe

“Moving a position can mean uprooting a family. It affects a spouse’s employment, children’s schooling, healthcare, and years of planning. HR should provide clear options, deadlines, and coordinated support. Leaders must own the follow-through,” Carrillo said.

Most U.S. tech giants are navigating the challenges arising from changing visa norms under Donald Trump’s leadership.

“IBM has an advantage because it already operates international offices with the infrastructure and staff to absorb those workers,” Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, told Rest of World . “Rather than abandoning the talent, companies like IBM can move the work to where the talent is.”

Earlier this year, Amazon allowed stranded H-1B workers to work from India amid consular delays but only temporarily. Microsoft defended its international talent hiring strategy in an October blog post pushing back against the U.S. administration’s allegations that it replaces American workers with foreign visa holders. The statement followed its suspension from the Department of Labor’s PERM green card program alongside Adobe and six other IT outsourcing firms, including TCS and Infosys.

“Companies are looking for solutions, but they’re also making business decisions,” Cassandra Fultz, co-founder of Doherty Fultz Immigration, told Rest of World . “Sponsoring an employee indefinitely, particularly when the outcome is uncertain, can be expensive and disruptive. Moving that employee to an existing operation abroad may be an option with more stability for the business. That doesn’t mean every employee will be offered the opportunity for placement abroad. Each country has its own eligibility requirements and work authorization rules. Companies will inevitably prioritize the people and positions they consider most valuable or difficult to replace.”

Even employees are reevaluating the lure of the American Dream as the uncertainty tax of constant visa changes weighs heavily on them. The wait for green cards for Indian nationals — who typically receive three-quarters of the H-1B visas and comprise the majority of the green card queue — can take several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy . Even with Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, immigration issues will stay with the White House and executive agencies.

“Mid-career professionals in the queue for green cards are most impacted,” Abhijit Bhaduri, former general manager for global learning and development at Microsoft and author of the upcoming book AIdentity: How to Become Irreplaceable in the New World of Work , told Rest of World . “They built a life in a country that still lists them as temporary. A visa is a document. But the vanishing green card queue feels like a broken promise. They followed every rule for years, and the finish line moved. You can relocate a job overnight. Rebuilding and redesigning a new identity takes years. That is the invisible price that gets missed.”

How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won't be easy

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

The promise and peril of AI in government

In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.

stories.body:
Several members of the group chat set up after the alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from their home towns in China

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered earlier this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they were contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.

Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the following day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company .

The group’s chat history, seen by the Guardian, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group their parents or themselves had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the following day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.

Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.

HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police from China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.

More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC .

Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.

Wang said the police seemed unaware the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, they threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China, she said.

“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China’,” Wang said.

Jack*, who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.

Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, global spokeswoman for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.

Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.

She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou , and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously stated that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said that if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.

after newsletter promotion

WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes over wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.

“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. However, these workers were usually working for projects by China’s state companies.

Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.

“Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”

The opposition home affairs spokesman, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.

The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.

The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

stories.summary: The party had boycotted full Senedd meetings after a member's speaking ban over remarks about immigration.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform's Welsh leader Helen Jenner says her party wants a vote to force the Senedd's presiding officer to quit

Published 24 November 2026, 14:57 GMT

Reform UK has ended a two-week boycott at the Senedd and says it wants a vote to remove the parliament's presiding officer.

The party's Members of the Senedd (MSs) have not contributed to full meetings of the Welsh Parliament since one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration.

A source close to Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies "wholly refuted" accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber.

Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon . Martin was not among them.

Reform's leader in Wales, Helen Jenner, began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us?"

"It's been a little bit duller without us in here," she added.

In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram".

This video can not be played

Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon

Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November.

The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech.

The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised.

Reform submitted a motion to remove the presiding officer, also known as the Llywydd, which could be voted on as early as Tuesday evening.

Huw Irranca-Davies told Reform MS Joe Martin he had to apologise before he could speak in the Senedd chamber

There is no indication the vote will get the support it needs from other parties to pass.

Shortly after its members had returned to the Senedd chamber, the party sent journalists a statement from Jenner.

She said the party "thought we were approaching a sensible resolution" in talks with the Llywydd that would allow Martin "to return to the chamber without apologising for the speech he made in the Senedd".

"It has become clear this morning that the Llywydd has not been negotiating in good faith and has changed his mind at the eleventh hour," Jenner said.

"He has admitted to us that his decisions on this matter have been influenced by the feelings of outside organisations.

"It is now for him to explain to the people of Wales which organisations they are and what that means for Welsh democracy.

"We now have no choice but to escalate this situation."

Jenner says her party has "no choice but to escalate this situation" following talks with the presiding officer

The Senedd's authorities strongly denied Reform's "completely inaccurate" claims and said the Llywydd's position had remained the same since he ruled against Martin.

A source close to Irranca-Davies said he was "always clear" during four meetings with Reform that Martin needed to apologise.

Irranca-Davies, who chairs Senedd plenary sessions, left the chamber during First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for the Llywydd said he met Jenner "entirely in good faith and had hoped to continue these confidential discussions constructively".

"It is unfortunate that they have chosen this course of action," the spokesperson added.

"While the Llywydd is disappointed, he respects the democratic process.

"Just as members elected him to this role, it is right that they have the opportunity to decide whether he continue to have their confidence."

stories.title: EFF to Congress: Mass Surveillance Is Too Important to Shove into Must-Pass Bill
stories.summary: In June 2026, the surveillance authority Section 702 of FISA expired absent a consensus among lawmakers over the terms of its reauthorization . Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a letter with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill. The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. It should not be used as a vehicle to circumvent or to cut short this long-running bipartisan debate over Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, nor to force lawmakers to choose between supporting our national defense and ending warrantless spying on Americans. Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process.” You can read the entire letter here . Section 702 grants the government authority to compel a telecommunications company to hand over data to the National Security Agency (NSA) in an attempt to protect national security by monitoring communications overseas—but this is only a piece of what the law does. Because we live in a globalized world, communications between people in other countries and in the United States often gets hoovered up. Once it does, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and several other agencies give themselves permission to search through U.S. persons’ data without a warrant. This is unconstitutional, undermines our right to private communications, and creates a dangerous and potent tool for would-be despots who might use that communication to discriminate, marginalize, or punish people based on their identities and political beliefs. stories.title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
stories.summary: It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email , fly , spend money , use an Apple device *, or do signals intelligence . Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it? Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12 , any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless. One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service. While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI ( or to malicious hackers ), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse. Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Published 23 November 2026

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.

But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.

Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.

However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.

But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.

Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.

Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Published 1 day ago

The U-turn suggests Nvidia's board believe Huang is irreplaceable.

The 63-year-old, who co-founded the company in 1993, transformed it from a chipmaker for video and computer games to the semiconductor powerhouse it is today, making the chips used in AI systems.

It is now one the most valuable firms in the world. Some believed Huang's departure risked not only the future of Nvidia, but the wider AI industry given the position the company, under Huang, has in the financing of other tech firms.

This video can not be played

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

In a interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

"Probably so," Trump said.

Trump's personal Nvidia investments

Since returning last year to the White House, the president has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia.

Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

The BBC has contacted the White House.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang Published 1 day ago

Congress vows to investigate Nvidia and the Trump administration's role

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, Prof Stuart Russell, told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Concerns remain among US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible".

"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to give evidence before the Senate banking committee.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee in January, said the reinstatement was "reckless".

And the chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

stories.body:
The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change , which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN ), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation ) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration ( issued by Colombia’s then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Read more: What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).

We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.
