stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. Blanche: DoJ 'looked into' concerns about Jensen Huang's alleged affair with Chinese spy

Todd Blanche, the attorney general, defended his department’s activity related to Nvidia and Jensen Huang on Tuesday, telling reporters that they “looked into” concerns related to Huang’s alleged affair with a Chinese spy.

“What I said last week is that we were looking into it,” Blanche said during a press conference. “The FBI, law enforcement looks into things all the time. That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation; it doesn’t necessarily become an indictment; it just literally is that. It’s looking into things.”

Blanche largely declined to give reporters detailed information about the Justice Department’s (DOJ) probe into Huang and Nvidia . But he insisted Nvidia is a “good corporate citizen” and that the DOJ had no information indicating Huang had committed a crime.

“To the extent that the Department of Justice had information that [Huang] was committing crimes or something like this… that’s something I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.

But the attorney general became defensive when reporters pressed him about the Justice Department’s process for ensuring Huang had not violated any laws.

“What does that mean, ‘Had Huang been investigated?’ For what?… I don’t understand the question,” Blanche said in response to a reporter’s question.

At another point, Blanche told a reporter: “I don’t know what folks are asking about specifically… I don’t, I mean, you’re mocking me, but when you say ‘get to the bottom of what is there,’ what are you asking me about?”

DoJ and other agencies conclude Jensen Huang not a national security risk, Blanche says

Todd Blanche also indicated the DOJ reached a “collective consensus” with other agencies and departments to determine that Jensen Huang was not a national security risk.

“How we make that type of determination – there’s a whole bunch of ways. We’re using the intelligence community, the FBI, the information we know, we talk to witnesses,” Blanche said in response to a reporter’s question on Tuesday.

“I know there’s heightened focus on this situation, but that’s something that the law enforcement partners and that the leadership in this country, whether it’s Commerce, or Treasury, State Department, the attorney general – me – it’s a collective consensus that we reach all the time in all kinds of different cases, not just in this case.”

Analysis: the Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence

Donald Trump ’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view .

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang , was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio , the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship .

“ It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act ,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency. She added:

double quotation mark It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.

Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Read Robert’s fascinating analysis here:

Why is scandal-plagued Jensen Huang back at Nvidia? - podcast

Jensen Huang is apparently too big to fail – but what does that mean for the rest of us?

Just last week, Nvidia ’s board chair told investors that the company had no intention of reinstating Huang as CEO. On Monday, they turned a full about-face. The board voted unanimously to reinstall Huang, triggering a nearly $1tn surge in the company’s stock market valuation . Donald Trump took credit, telling CNBC that he “convinced them” to bring Huang back. But questions remain about Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and about whether Nvidia exploited loopholes to export chips to Chinese AI companies .

In today’s edition of our Stateside podcast, Kai Wright talks with the Guardian US’s tech editor Blake Montgomery about the many twists and turns in the Huang scandal – and why Huang embodies the “key man risk” that threatens our whole economy.

Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return

Julia Kollewe and Graeme Wearden

Donald Trump made up to $15m on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive .

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from the US president.

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.”

The US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times.

Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% on Monday, adding about $950bn to the company’s value. Huang returned to the company’s HQ in Santa Clara, California, receiving a hero’s welcome , with crowds of employees chanting “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”

Trump has bought Nvidia shares worth between $23m and $86m , according to a BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the past two years. He has also sold some of his stake in the company since returning to the presidency, and gained between $3.5m and $10.2m , according to his government disclosures.

Zohran Mamdani , New York City’s mayor, on Monday weighed in on the corporate turbulence surrounding Nvidia and the chipmaker’s CEO, Jensen Huang , saying he does not think working Americans “signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of … Huang’s fidelity to his marriage.”

The mayor said Huang “had a massive impact”, with Nvidia’s share price dropping dramatically when he stepped down as the company’s CEO on 12 November after a reported extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

But on Monday, after he was reinstated after Donald Trump intervened , the California-based company’s value bounced back by 31.5%.

Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang – who have been married since 1985 and have combined assets of about $160bn – have made no statement about their marriage in the wake of the reported affair. But at a news conference on Monday after Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, Mamdani took the opportunity to make a point about wealth.

“We’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumored to be around $81bn,” he said . “That would be the cost of providing universal childcare for every three- and four-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year.”

Alluding to Louis Brandeis, the late US supreme court justice who was at the forefront of an antitrust movement, Mamdani continued:

double quotation mark A lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is: We can have democracy. We can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few. We cannot have both.

Mamdani also made a point about the stock market. He said that market was “disproportionately dependent” on stocks related to the artificial intelligence boom powered by Nvidia’s chips. “It cannot help but give you a sense of concern about just how much this technology is now dominant,” he said.

“I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage,” Mamdani said. “And yet, for many days, that had a massive impact.”

House Dems call for Jensen Huang to testify at public hearing

Democrat Gregory Meeks , the ranking member on the House foreign affairs committee, has called on Jensen Huang to testify at a public committee hearing following Donald Trump ’s intervention to get him reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO and amid national security concerns raised by Huang’s efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China .

Meeks said in a statement : “Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security. President Trump’s intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA’s CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration’s own rol e, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public.

“For the past year, committee members have raised concerns about NVIDIA’s effort to weaken U.S. export restrictions on advanced chips sales to China , as well as widespread allegations regarding the diversion of NVIDIA chips from third countries to China . We have many questions surrounding the administration’s role in approving exports that have put America’s national security up for sale.

‘The American people deserve to hear publicly from Mr. Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played . A transcribed interview is critical to our oversight efforts but it should not replace a public hearing. Chairman Mast should convene one.”

Earlier we mentioned Donald Trump is participating in a Medal of Freedom ceremony in the Oval Office at 11am ET. He will be awarding the nation’s highest civilian honor to former New York mayor and Trump’s onetime personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani .

Trump said last year he would award the medal to Giuliani, two days after his longtime political ally was seriously injured in a car crash.

Giuliani was once lauded for leading New York after the September 11, 2001, attacks and later sanctioned by courts and disbarred for amplifying false claims about the 2020 US presidential election. Giuliani was also criminally charged in two states, and later pardoned by Trump , over his role in a plot to steal the 2020 election.

US preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries – report

The US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, the Wall Street Journal reports (paywall) this morning , citing people familiar with the plans.

Per the Journal’s report: “US trade representative Jamieson Greer as soon as this week is expected to unveil the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations , said the people, who warned the timing could change.

“Greer has said those subsidies and other governmental supports have created excess industrial capacity in the targeted economies, allowing their firms to flood global markets with cheaper goods, undermining US producers.”

As we noted earlier, Nvidia’s freshly reinstated CEO , Jensen Huang, will appear on Capitol Hill next week, where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill him over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China. Huang will also sit for transcribed interviews with the Senate banking committee and House foreign affairs committee, as well as the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee. (Here’s our Shrai Popat’s report ).

Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren , the incoming Senate banking chair, has told Politico Playbook: “President Trump insisting that the company should rehire him does not get Mr. Huang or Nvidia off the hook. ”

Asked whether Huang’s return changes the investigation, Warren replied without hesitation: “ Yes, and not to Nvidia’s benefit .”

“All the excuses of ‘I don’t know what Nvidia is doing now because I’m not there’ will be denied to Mr. Huang, ” Warren said, “ and Nvidia’s ability to separate itself from a CEO that is under serious investigation over whether [he] has participated in an international scandal of monumental proportions will also have disappeared .”

Huang and Nvidia “together makes very clear the need for a serious, independent investigation ”, Warren added.

Three bipartisan bills are ready to go, she outlined:

double quotation mark Don’t sell these chips to China. Don’t sell the equipment to make these chips to China, and every chip that leaves the United States should have a tracker on it.

Huang “will have to answer Republican and Democratic members of the Banking Committee”, Warren said, “on why he actively lobbied to send Nvidia’s chips to China and whether Nvidia’s chips have been smuggled to fuel China’s military ”. She added: “ I’ll be pressing for that. But I won’t be the only one. ”

Iran ’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf reiterated on Tuesday that Tehran would not hold talks with the United States until Iran’s seven conditions are met.

“ Our position remains what we have previously stated: There will be no actions or negotiations until Iran’s seven conditions are met ,” Iran’s chief negotiator said in a report carried by the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency.

He also warned:

double quotation mark Furthermore, we are prepared to respond decisively to any hostile moves by the enemy and, should the enemy commit a miscalculation, to shift the geography of the conflict .

Tehran’s conditions include sanctions relief, lifting the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, releasing seized Iranian assets, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

It comes as the naval arm of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said three oil tankers were struck naval mines in strait of Hormuz because they were “in violation of regulations” regarding passage through the waterway.

The Guard’s navy said in a post on Telegram on Monday that the strait “is not a place to test unauthorized routes or to disregard maritime warnings”.

It said the tankers were “engulfed in flames” after hitting the mines despite being under US aerial escort.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday that all three vessels continued their transits and all crew were accounted for.

Donald Trump will take part in a Medal of Freedom ceremony in the Oval Office at 11am ET this morning, it’s closed to press but we’ll let you know if it opens up. Then at 2pm he and the first lady will participate in the Thanksgiving turkey pardoning at the White House, this year featuring turkeys Freedom and Feather. The president will then do a print interview before departing for Palm Beach, where he’ll spend Thanksgiving.

Juliana Stratton, the incoming Democratic senator from Illinois , said she would support significantly reforming or abolishing the filibuster in order to allow Congress to deliver on the promises they made American voters.

The filibuster means that most successful legislation in the Senate must have 60 supporters instead of a simple majority. Eliminating that requirement is one of several reforms Democrats can act on after they won an unexpected 56-44 majority in the next US Senate, their largest majority in nearly two decades.

Stratton, currently the Illinois lieutenant governor, was a professional mediator before she entered politics. For two decades, she ran a dispute resolution firm, bringing people who did not agree together to find ways to solve problems.

The experience will serve her well in a divided government, she told the Guardian. She welcomes Republicans who want to stand up to Trump and “have a real spine” to work with and Democrats in the US Senate .

“We cannot go in kind of waffling on, ‘Well, we’ll see what we can do, it’s going to be hard.’ That’s the same kind of thing that really turned so many voters off this election cycle – people going in, telling them how hard everything is and that there’s so many hurdles,” Stratton said. “Sure, there are hurdles, but we were elected to do hard things.”

House Democrat expands investigation into Donald Trump Jr's investment firm

A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr ’s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies, AP reports.

Representative Jamie Raskin , the ranking member of the House judiciary committee and the panel’s incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.

The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years’ worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether president Donald Trump’s eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances.

US envoy 'not certain' military aid to Israel will end this year as Trump promised

Mike Huckabee, the US ⁠ambassador to Israel , ⁠has cast doubt ​on whether Washington would end its $3.8bn in annual military aid to Israel by the end of this year, as promised by Donald Trump on the day ⁠of this month’s midterm elections.

In his surprise announcement as voters headed to the polls on 3 November, Trump said he had made a deal with prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu several months earlier ⁠to stop providing Israel with about $4bn in annual US funding.

Trump said Israel no longer needed US funds, and ​the issue had been used as a “bad talking point” by ‌his leftwing critics, Reuters reported.

The election that ‌day subsequently saw Democrats, including many who publicly oppose military funding for Israel, win control of both houses of Congress ‌from Trump’s Republicans .

Trump did not provide details or explain how the funding would be halted. The US has a longstanding agreement with Israel, known as a memorandum of understanding, to provide it with $3.8bn a year until 2028 to fund purchases of American-made military equipment.

Congress to grill Jensen Huang over ties with China and Trump’s intervention

Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive is “exhibit A” of the “political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy”, Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat vying to become the next Senate majority leader, told reporters Monday.

Van Hollen said he intends to focus on Huang’s “efforts to increase and accelerate the export of high-end chips to China, how he’s been accomplishing that, how he’s been getting his way with the administration” when the reinstalled Nvidia CEO appears before the Senate banking committee on 3 December.

It will be one of several appearances on Capitol Hill next week where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill Huang over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China . Huang will also sit for transcribed interviews with the House foreign affairs committee, as well as the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee.

“It’s completely hypocritical for the Trump administration, on the one hand, to say the reason we have to take all the brakes off AI development here at home is because China will leap ahead if we don’t,” Van Hollen said. “When in fact, it’s the Trump administration that’s helping China leap ahead.”

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang after Donald Trump intervened on the executive’s behalf, assuring company leadership that he did not pose a national security risk despite questions surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, a tech executive of no relation who has been accused of acting as a Chinese asset and routing advanced chips to Beijing via her data center company, Megaspeed.

In an interview with CNBC on Monday, the US president defended his involvement in Huang’s reinstatement, arguing it would be a “bigger threat” for Nvidia to lose Huang’s “brain power” in the AI race. Trump also confirmed that he had provided the board with assurances regarding any national security concerns.

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them,” Trump said.

Democrats criticise Nvidia after Trump's intervention sees CEO Huang resinstated

“We also have to figure out how corporate America doesn’t take a bad lesson from this, and thinks that somehow it’s OK for them to evade national security for the purposes of just selling more,” Gallego, an Arizona Democrat considering a White House campaign, said.

Meanwhile, California representative Ro Khanna wrote on social media that “rules should apply to everyone”, noting: “The rich + powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price.”

Huang returned to the company’s HQ in Santa Clara, California, on Monday and received a hero’s welcome , with crowds of employees chanting “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”

Donald Trump made up to $15m on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Huang .

His return as CEO came despite Huang being subject to several government and internal investigations, shareholder lawsuits and accusations that he’s a national security threat.

Nvidia is one of the most valuable businesses in the world, worth about $4tn, and the entire AI ecosphere relies on it. The company engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power tech firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.

In other developments:

Speaking at the US Department of Justice, Trump railed against the commutations of death row inmates’ sentences by California’s governor, Gavin Newsom. Jimmy Gomez will resign from Congress after a House ethics report released on Monday found “substantial evidence” that the California Democrat had “engaged in sexual misconduct”, including by “making unwelcome sexual advances and sexual contact toward a House staffer”. State-run Global Times says reports about CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy were ‘malicious’

Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return

Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?

Chinese media have reacted with glee to the dramatic reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, with one commentary warning against future “witch-hunts”.

An article published on Tuesday in the state-run outlet the Global Times said US media reports about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset were “malicious” and “negatively impacted American public perception of China”.

Huang was reinstated to the US artificial intelligence company on Tuesday, weeks after he was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs , including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from Donald Trump.

The Global Times warned that future “political witch-hunts” against companies and individuals accused of links to Chinese intelligence could take the form of investigations and congressional hearings.

“Certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering [sic],” it said.

In another article, the influential blogger Niu Tanqin wrote that Huang’s return indicated that the “so-called female spy allegations are complete nonsense”.

Niu also said that China would be flattered by Donald Trump’s suggestion, made in an interview with CNBC, that Huang could be poached by China.

The US president said on Monday that Xi Jinping, China’s leader, described Huang as a “brilliant man” in their recent meeting in Shenzhen, a city in southern China.

Trump said that, despite the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s affair with the alleged China intelligence asset Alice Huang – no relation – “the bigger threat would be losing the brainpower of somebody like Jensen”.

Nvidia produces the world’s most advanced semiconductors, which underpin the artificial intelligence sector. US export controls have blocked Nvidia from shipping its most sophisticated models to China in a bid to slow down the country’s AI development. Huang has pushed for looser regulations, arguing that it is better to keep China dependent on US technology rather than spur Chinese innovation.

Trump said he had personally intervened with the Nvidia board, which had previously ruled out reinstating Huang. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.”

Huang’s comeback caused Nvidia’s shares to soar on Monday, adding almost $1tn (£763bn) in market value to the company, which props up much of the US stock markets.

Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chair of the intelligence committee, said : “I have warned the administration from the start about communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry declined to comment on Huang’s reinstatement. The government has consistently denied the espionage allegations, calling them “slander and defamation”.

Several accounts on Chinese social media shared memes and AI-generated videos showing Huang in various revenge scenarios. In one video, shared by an influential blogger, with more than 1.1 million followers, Huang is reimagined in the Arnold Schwarzenegger movie The Terminator, in the famous “I’ll be back” scene.

In another video, Huang is reimagined as Jack Nicholson’s murderous Jack Torrance in the 1980 horror film The Shining. Huang is shown using an axe to destroy a locked bathroom door, terrorising an AI-generated Colette Kress, who was Nvidia’s interim boss , who is cowering behind it. The video ends with an AI-generated “Here’s Jensen!” channelling Nicholson’s famous line, “Here’s Johnny!”, from the movie.

Analysts believe that the saga also demonstrated to Beijing how power works in the US.

“The lesson Chinese policymakers are likely drawing is neither subtle nor complicated: Donald Trump remains the most influential political figure in America and, in many respects, the most consequential variable in the trajectory of US-China relations,” wrote George Chen, a partner at The Asia Group, a consultancy, in a post on Substack.

stories.body:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang , was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geo-strategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other Southeast Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.

“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”

Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided with the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the defense intelligence agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.

“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg , a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”

The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”

No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling Ministry of State Security [MSS] is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.

Frank Montoya, a retired Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multi-billion dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”

The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spy craft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore data centers to Chinese AI companies, Curlew argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang, and her links to Chinese intelligence is thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering Shenzhen.

It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

stories.body:
The US and Russia lack the power to impose their will on the continent – the Shenzhen summit was no Yalta 2.0

T he first ever trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin was rich in symbolism and empty of substance. Many Europeans, filled with anxiety about the Chinese, Russian and US presidents potentially colluding, saw chilling echoes of the Yalta conference in 1945, when Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt redrew the map of Europe.

But those – particularly in eastern Europe – who are fretting about another historic betrayal should remember that when it comes to European security today, we are the ones who hold most of the cards. Far more meaningful last week than Shenzhen was a gathering in Berlin , held at exactly the same time.

True, the Shenzhen summit brought together three autocratic leaders who would like to see the world carved up into spheres of influence, but their meeting turned out to be no Yalta 2.0. The original Yalta took place as the second world war drew to a close, when international law and multilateral organisations were little more than a pipedream. The world was still living in an age of empire, with many colonies in the hands of European countries and the Soviet Union eager to consolidate its own in eastern Europe . It was hardly surprising, back then, that the war’s victors, the US, the UK and the USSR, held the keys to Europe’s future.

Nothing of the kind was ever going to happen in Shenzhen, nor will it at any future gathering of Xi, Trump and Putin alone. Two of the three – Putin and Trump – cannot win the wars they have launched against Ukraine and Iran respectively. The third, Xi, by far the strongest of the trio, is doing little more than bask in the colossal mistakes of his American and Russian friends.

This is not to say that the three are irrelevant to Europe’s security. Russia and the US hold the world’s largest nuclear arsenals. Had Trump, Putin and Xi committed to nuclear arms control, as Trump wanted , Europe (and the rest of the world) would have applauded. But the Russian and Chinese leaders were never going to indulge Trump on that score. Possessing nuclear weapons is the only reason Putin can still claim a seat at the top table; without them, Russia would be little more than a second-rate power. China, meanwhile, in its scramble for superpower status, is racing to expand its nuclear arsenal, and catch up with the US and Russia.

Russia, China and the US also matter in other dimensions of security. Putin’s Russia continues its military assault on Ukraine, which faces its hardest winter since Russia invaded. And Russia’s cyber-attacks, drone incursions, sabotage, attacks on critical infrastructure and disinformation campaigns across Europe have escalated to the point that it makes little sense to keep talking about “hybrid war”, or even “shadow war”. It would perhaps be more honest simply to call it what it is: Russia’s war against Europe.

Russia is hardly fighting this war alone. China is not a direct participant, but has provided economic and technological support that has been vital to Russia’s war machine. Yet for all their efforts, there is no sign that Ukraine, or indeed any other European country, will fold – and this despite the fact that Trump’s US has all but switched sides. Washington no longer provides economic or military support to Ukraine. And while it still cooperates on intelligence and satellite communications, it has sickeningly tried to pressure Kyiv into capitulating by temporarily cutting off or slowing down these services. The US still has the capacity to inflict real damage on Ukraine and Europe. But Trump has failed to subjugate Ukraine over the last two years, and given his Republican party’s bruising defeat in the US midterm elections, he is unlikely to succeed in the next two.

Trump, Putin and Xi may like a world in which, to borrow from Thucydides, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Their agreement in Shenzhen to oppose the alleged overreach of international tribunals – established precisely to disprove that might makes right – signals exactly this. But the three men are not as strong as they would like to believe, nor is today’s world the Hobbesian wasteland over which Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin had the power to rule unchallenged. International law and multilateralism are under attack – but they are not dead. Middle powers in the global south are rising and making their voices heard.

after newsletter promotion

And Europe, though facing serious security threats, has far more leverage than is often recognised. Last week’s meeting in Berlin – where representatives of 36 countries in the French- and British-led coalition of the willing gathered to shore up support for Ukraine – was a show of strength far more concrete than the empty words in Shenzhen.

The group agreed to close Ukraine’s funding gap for 2027: the EU has pledged an additional €45bn , with a further €25bn coming from non-EU coalition members such as the UK, Norway and Canada. And while the last time the EU agreed on a loan to Ukraine guaranteed by the EU budget, it allowed Hungary and Slovakia to opt out, today it is in no mood to tolerate dropouts. With negotiations on the next seven-year EU budget entering a critical phase, Germany, the largest net contributor, will oppose any budget deal unless all EU members agree to support Ukraine.

Europe’s main problem is not material but political and, above all, psychological. Learned helplessness, towards the US in particular, is what fuels fears of the ghosts of Yalta, and a new betrayal. And it is because Europe still takes the Trump-Putin peace-talks charade too seriously that it spends so much time squabbling over who should represent it at that table.

No peace plan pushed through by Putin and Trump will deliver Ukraine’s surrender, let alone a new security architecture for Europe. On their own, they lack the power to impose their will. The more energy Europe devotes to delivering on the plans and pledges of the coalition of the willing, and the less it spends chasing the two failing leaders in Moscow and Washington, the more secure and peaceful tomorrow’s Europe will be.

stories.body:
After the president’s meeting with Putin and Xi, the US must take the lead in restoring arms control agreements

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping met last week in southern China, where Trump said they would “talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization”.

It was the first time the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers had come together to discuss the future of nuclear weapons. That discussion was long overdue.

But in typical Trump fashion, this meeting was all pomp and little pop. If Trump wants to make the world safer, he needs to do more than talk. The US needs to lead.

Nuclear weapons remain the greatest immediate threat to the security of the US, Russia, China and the entire world. As the risks of artificial intelligence, climate emergency and geopolitical instability grow, the danger of nuclear catastrophe has not diminished. In fact, the erosion of arms control agreements and the modernization and expansion of nuclear arsenals are bringing us closer to a dangerous new arms race.

The first priority must be rebuilding the arms control architecture that the United States and Russia spent half a century constructing. During and after the cold war, Washington and Moscow negotiated a series of treaties that helped prevent nuclear confrontation and reduced their nuclear arsenals by roughly 88%.

Those agreements demonstrated that even adversaries can find common ground when the stakes are existential.

But that progress is now in jeopardy.

The New Start Treaty, the last remaining agreement limiting the strategic nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia, expired earlier this year without a replacement. Today, there are no legally binding limits on the size of their nuclear arsenals and China has never been subject to comparable restrictions.

The result is a growing risk of a three-way nuclear arms race that would make all three countries – and the world – less safe.

There were plenty of reasons to be skeptical that this meeting could produce meaningful results. Trump likes to talk about “denuclearization”, but talk is not a strategy.

During his first administration, Trump tried to bring China into bilateral nuclear arms control negotiations between Washington and Moscow. That effort failed because Beijing correctly pointed out that it had a much smaller arsenal than the others.

China is expanding its nuclear arsenal, but it possesses roughly 600 nuclear weapons, compared with approximately 4,000 in the arsenals of both the US and Russia. Expecting Beijing to negotiate reductions on the same terms as Washington and Moscow is simply unrealistic. We cannot make progress by demanding that China reduce its arsenal while the US and Russia retain arsenals many times larger.

Nor should Trump wait for Putin to make the first move. Putin has increasingly relied on nuclear threats to discourage other countries from supporting Ukraine and to advance his broader strategic objectives. But even though he may resist reductions, that does not mean Russia wants to spend the next decade locked in another costly nuclear arms race.

In fact, shortly before New Start expired, Moscow proposed that the United States and Russia voluntarily maintain their existing limits on strategic nuclear weapons while negotiating a successor agreement. Trump rejected that proposal.

That was a missed opportunity. Trump should reverse course and put that proposal back on the table.

If Trump wants to make real progress, he needs to change his tune and lead the band. He should immediately agree with Putin to freeze their nuclear arsenals while negotiating a new arms control agreement to replace New Start.

And we should aim higher than simply restoring the status quo. A new agreement should reduce American and Russian nuclear arsenals to 1,000 weapons each, counting both strategic (long-range) weapons and tactical (shorter-range) weapons. Such reductions would lower the risk of nuclear war, rebuild a measure of trust between Washington and Moscow, and save taxpayers billions of dollars that would otherwise be spent building and maintaining weapons we do not need.

Just as importantly, a serious American-Russian agreement would create the conditions for China to join the process. Beijing should commit to refraining from further significant increases in its nuclear arsenal as long as Washington and Moscow are making real progress toward substantial reductions.

The objective should be straightforward: bring American and Russian arsenals down toward China’s level, not drive China to build up toward ours. That is how we prevent a three-way arms race before it gets started.

Some will argue that the United States must maintain nuclear superiority over China and should never reduce its arsenal unless Beijing agrees to comparable reductions. But that approach mistakes nuclear superiority for nuclear security.

History demonstrates that arms control works when countries negotiate from a position of mutual security and seek stability, rather than endlessly pursuing an advantage over one another.

A new nuclear arms race among the US, Russia and China would serve nobody’s interests. It would waste enormous sums of public money, accelerate environmental damage, undermine international security and increase the possibility that a crisis or miscalculation could end in nuclear catastrophe.

The world does not need another nuclear arms race. It needs leadership, diplomacy, and a clear commitment to a safer future. If Trump is serious about denuclearization, moving forward, he now has his chance to prove it.

Edward J Markey represents Massachusetts in the US Senate. He is a co-chair of the bicameral congressional nuclear weapons and arms control working group

Temporary quotas on vehicles entering the bloc tariff-free will also apply to cars from the UK, Japan and Turkey

Business live – latest updates

The EU will next month impose its threatened caps on the number of Chinese hybrid cars that can be imported into the bloc without facing a tariff, the European Commission has announced.

The quotas will also apply to hybrids from Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the UK, but the principal purpose is to limit imports from China after an agreement with Beijing in October that has led to a rise in exports to the bloc.

The quota, under World Trade Organization rules, is temporary and will apply for 200 days from 1 December during an investigation into imports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid vehicles. The EU is attempting to cut its huge trade deficit with China.

“In view of the sensitivity of the hybrids sector, its strategic importance to the union economy in terms of innovation, electrification and employment, and the existence of sufficient evidence showing that imports of hybrids threaten to cause serious injury to the union industry,” the official journal said on Tuesday.

It will limit tariff-free imports of Chinese vehicles to 350,000 in the first year or about 191,000 over 200 days.

First-year quotas would be set at 310,000 for Japan, 230,000 for Turkey, 105,000 for South Korea and 190,000 for the UK, which last year exported 166,000 hybrids to the EU.

The quota amounts to about half of the number of Chinese hybrids expected to be imported to the EU in the next 12 months.

Figures in the journal showed that imports of Chinese EVs rocketed from 21,000 units in 2020 to 438,000 in 2024 when tariffs were imposed.

After the tariffs were imposed, imports of EVs began to “flatten out”, with a “clear shift” from EVs to hybrids from China , it said.

Worldwide exports of hybrids from China rocketed from 191,000 vehicles in 2023 to 1.124m in 2025, the EU said.

To head off “the likelihood of substantially increased imports into the union”, the EU now is imposing a quota.

The volume limits are “safeguard” measures that have to apply to all big exporters of ‌hybrid cars to the EU. Other countries to which the import caps apply are South Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Serbia and the US, but they are most restrictive for China.

after newsletter promotion

According to industry reports, non-EU countries including the UK have questioned the allocations.

At a WTO goods council meeting last week, South Korea questioned whether the investigation was fair and transparent. Japan, the UK, Switzerland and Turkey stressed transparency and due process.

China’s commerce ministry said it hoped the EU would abide by the consensus the two sides had reached, and that it reserved all rights to firmly safeguard the legitimate interests of Chinese industries.

The European Commission said imports from China came not just at the expense of EU production, but were also eating into the market shares of other exporters such as Japan and South Korea.

The UK is still fighting against a 10% tariff on all exports of EVs to China, due to come into force on 1 January under the 2020 Brexit trade and cooperation deal.

It has now been intrinsically linked to Andy Burnham’s attempts to get the UK classified as a European manufacturer in the EU’s still-to-be-finalised “Made in Europe” scheme , which protects against cheap Chinese imports.
