stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
CEO behind Nvidia’s meteoric rise stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then was reinstated days later

Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. The announcement of his resignation came on 12 November. A week and a half later, he was reinstated as the chief executive in a unanimous vote by Nvidia’s board.

Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.

China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns.

Initially, it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. Reuters later reported a third affair, this one with another Nvidia employee.

How did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.

2023

March 2023 Megaspeed, a datacenter firm, is spun out from a Chinese video game company

Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg.

November 2023 Megaspeed is sold to a Singaporean shell company and becomes an Nvidia cloud partner

Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry.

Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

2024

June 2024 Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are seen together in Taipei, Taiwan

Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal.

2024 to 2025 Megaspeed receives hundreds of shipments of Nvidia AI chips

The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Alibaba.

September 2024 The US Department of Commerce begins investigating Megaspeed

The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips.

2025

January 2025 Jensen Huang meets Donald Trump for the first time

Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office.

April 2025 Jensen Huang attends a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago

The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.

May 2025 Jensen Huang is again seen with Alice Huang

The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reports that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier.

October 2025 Trump is reportedly briefed on the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang

The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this.

December 2025 Trump approves the sale of more advanced Nvidia chips to China

Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second-most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government.

2026

May 2026 Marco Rubio reportedly drafts a memo about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip.

October 2026 The New York Times reports Jensen Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese spy

At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary.

8 November 2026 Jensen Huang admits to having an affair

In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement.

Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished .

9 November 2026 Trump says he is ‘amazed’ by the allegations that Alice Huang is a spy

At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”.

“And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’

“I really believe him,” Trump says.

10 November 2026 A shareholder in California files a lawsuit against Nvidia and its CEO

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.

11 November 2026 The New York Times reports there was a second affair, and the Nvidia board reportedly prepares to oust Huang

The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare.

At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO.

12 November 2026 Jensen Huang steps down as CEO of Nvidia

Huang steps down, effectively ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO.

Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

17 November 2026 Nvidia’s board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang

Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chair of the company’s board says. Harvey Jones makes the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announces the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago.

23 November 2026 Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO

Nvidia reinstates Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal. The company’s shares surge on the news, jumping 33% and adding more than $1tn to its market value.

Donald Trump, who had called for Huang’s return, trumpets his own involvement in negotiations with Nvidia’s board to return the former CEO to his position. The president says, “the country needs Jensen’s leadership” and that the US government has no “evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct”.

In a statement , the board says it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.

stories.body:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.

The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.

The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.

The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.

stories.title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
stories.summary: A government-commissioned report calls for a "rebalancing" of the amount paid to different claimants.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 14 minutes ago

The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.

The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.

The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.

The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".

Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings.

The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.

The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.

It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.

Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit Published 4 hours ago

Giving a statement in the House of Commons, Sir Stephen said Pip "remains a vital source of support" but the system was "no longer fit for purpose".

He told MPs the current assessment process was "dehumanising" and focused on "what somebody cannot do", rather than "supporting independence".

The government has committed to a recommendation that people receiving end-of-life care or with "serious, well-evidenced conditions" would receive payments without a full assessment.

It has also agreed to reduce "unnecessary" reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve.

Under the report's proposals, cash payments would remain alongside better support to signpost people into education or employment, although claimants could choose to exchange part of their payment for practical services instead.

In the longer-term, the report recommends changes to the assessment process that look at someone's real-life additional costs and individual needs, focusing on "how people can live the life they want to live, rather than what they cannot do".

It proposes "improved" questions to understand the extra costs people face, although claimants would not be asked to calculate their costs or provide receipts.

'Rebalancing'

Currently eligibility for Pip is based on how difficult people find carrying out everyday tasks, with two levels of payment available.

But the review suggests future payment options could include bands more closely linked to extra costs.

The report says its approach is likely to lead to a "rebalancing" of payments, indicating that some claimants could lose out under a new system, either receiving less than they do currently or not qualifying for payments at all.

"Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support," it says.

"Conversely, this benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled."

The review also calls for an increase in face-to-face assessments, which has been show to reduce eligibility.

The remit of the review was not to produce savings, and it does not set out whether the reforms would reduce the overall welfare bill.

Spending on Pip is set to be about £32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to £41.5bn by the end of the decade.

It comes after a separate review by former minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

The government welcomed Milburn's report , which included a recommendation to move under-25s off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

This has lead to concerns about a two-tier system, where some people with the same conditions could get different levels of payments depending on their age.

The government has said it will consider the Timms review alongside Milburn's recommendations, with its final proposals set out early next year.

Sir Stephen said this would include detailing the overall costs of changes to the system.

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 7 days ago

'Months of uncertainty'

Eduin Latimer, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said the review's recommendations had "the potential to better tailor Pip to claimants' needs".

But he said this would also create challenges, "most importantly in defining what disability-related costs are included, and finding a fair way of measuring them".

Latimer said making it easier to apply for Pip in its current form would "likely increase the number of claimants - and hence spending".

He added: "If the government wants to make Pip easier to apply for while also keeping spending in line with current projections, they would likely have to tighten eligibility criteria or reduce award amounts."

Disability charities have largely welcomed the review's recommendations of fast-tracked support and fewer reassessments.

However, they have said any changes should not leave disabled people financially worse off.

The Liberal Democrats said younger disabled people would now face "months of uncertainty" whilst the government considers the separate reviews from Timms and Milburn, and urged ministers to say quickly what they intend to do.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales. However, the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

stories.title: Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit
stories.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has published his review of the personal independence payment (Pip), along with recommended changes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

A review of the main disability benefit has recommended an overhaul of the system to allow disabled people to "achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence".

The report proposes both short and long terms changes to the personal independence payment (Pip) for claimants in England and Wales.

The benefit is claimed by four million people and is available to people whether they are in work or unemployed. Its aim is to help with the additional costs of being disabled.

Here's what you need to know.

Pip benefit system 'not fit for purpose' and 'dehumanising' assessments should change, review finds - follow live

The current Pip process does not work

This is the first review of the benefit since it was introduced in 2013. More than 40,000 disabled people engaged with the process with more than 90% of them saying they'd had a negative experience while applying for Pip, describing it as stressful, dehumanising or psychologically damaging. The review concludes the Pip process is "not fit for purpose" and calls for a fundamental redesign.

While the review was chaired by Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, the experience of disabled people is clear throughout the review.

The review recommends both short and long term changes

First the short term.

A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.

Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.

Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.

Then the long term.

Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.

Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.

A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.

The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.

The review does not propose benefits cuts

The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's.

The report says that a reformed Pip system that more accurately reflects peoples' needs will likely mean "a rebalancing process". While the review didn't set out to make savings, it couldn't increase the overall costs and with some people likely to gain, others will almost certainly lose some cash. The review is not explicit on who these people might be.

Separate research last month from a think tank, the Resolution Foundation, suggested that one in six Pip recipients didn't have any additional costs associated with their conditions. In an interview to coincide with the review, Timms said that "if people don't have extra costs, then this is not the benefit for them".

How does this report sit with the Milburn review that was published last week?

Alan Milburn's report - which proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK - recommended that Pip be removed from people under 25 as part of a package of measures to tackle youth unemployment.

Today's review does not make the same recommendation. It will be up to the government to decide how they marry the two reports. They have said they are committed to reforming the Pip assessment process, but what that means in practice probably won't be known until the New Year when they publish their considered response.

stories.title: Tory plan to sell off London's Victorian jails to raise £1.4bn
stories.summary: The party says the move could fund the construction of modern purpose-built prisons elsewhere.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Wandsworth prison, in south London, is among those that would be closed by the Conservatives

Published 3 hours ago

London's Victorian jails should be closed down and the land sold off to property developers, the Conservatives have said, as they launched a plan to massively increase prison places in England and Wales.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said the move could raise £1.4bn to help fund the construction of "modern, purpose-built prisons elsewhere".

He claimed a Tory government would create 50,000 extra prison places within "six or seven years" and end Labour's early release scheme in its first term in office.

Labour said nobody would believe the Tory plan "given they only added a dismal 500 places while in government".

Speaking at a press conference in Westminster, Timothy said it was "fair" to highlight the previous Conservartive government's failure to significantly increase prison places.

But he insisted "this is a different generation of Conservative politicians under Kemi [Badenoch]'s leadership, and we are making different choices".

Unlike previous Tory-led administrations, they were being "explicit" about which departmental budgets they would cut - international aid, culture and the Cabinet Office - to fund new prisons, he added.

Under the Tory plans, an extra £2bn a year would go to the Ministry of Justice to pay for what Timothy called "the largest prison-building programme in modern history".

"It will let us end Labour's early release schemes once and for all, and bring back shorter sentences to lock up criminals like shoplifters," he added.

He told the audience "prison works" because it kept criminals off the street and he was "deeply sceptical about talk of rehabilitation".

The Conservatives are setting up a commission, chaired by former minister Sir Simon Clarke, to work out how to speed up the building of new prisons by removing obstacles in the planning, procurement and judicial systems.

The review would also look at "how to get out of the old Victorian prison estate, starting in London," Timothy said in his speech.

Prisons such as Wormwood Scrubs, Brixton, Wandsworth and Pentonville "sit on some of the most valuable land in the world," he added.

"Getting out of these sites is not only a good idea in itself. It will free up land for residential use in London, where our housing shortage is most acute."

He said the Tories would "strip back regulations, like affordable housing quotas and listed status, to give the land its highest realisable value," but it would only sell off the land when "market conditions are favourable to the taxpayer".

This could raise more than £1.4bn which would go towards building new prisons "in addition to" the 50,000 places the party has already pledged to build , he added.

The previous Conservative government set out plans to sell off London's Victorian jails, but this was ditched by Boris Johnson's administration in 2019 because of the shortage of prison places.

A Labour spokesperson said: "When it comes to leaving the prisons estate on the verge of collapse, the Tories are guilty as charged.

"They should be apologising to victims of crime who they badly let down rather than spending time lecturing others who are fixing the mess they left behind."

The Labour government was "delivering the largest prison building programme since the Victorian era so victims of crime get the justice they deserve," they added.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Delegation of 50 to accompany minister, with trip criticised after universities were warned about Chinese interference

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, is travelling to Beijing this week to promote UK education, weeks after MI5 issued a rare public warning to universities about Chinese interference in UK academia.

A 50-strong UK delegation, including 18 university leaders, will accompany the minister when she attends the first UK-China education summit in nine years, aimed at opening up new opportunities for universities, colleges and education businesses.

The visit prompted criticism, as it comes two months after UK universities were warned by MI5 that China’s intelligence services were using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal secrets from hi-tech projects.

One critic described Powell’s visit, which begins on Tuesday, as “mind-blowingly shortsighted”, while the Conservatives said the education secretary’s priorities were “all wrong”.

Discussions in China are expected to cover higher education, technical and vocational education, schools, English language teaching, digital education and education technology, the Department for Education (DfE) said

“The freedom and independence of our academic institutions is sacrosanct,” a DfE spokesperson said. “We will not accept collaborations which compromise our national security or attempt to benefit covertly from research done in partnership with UK universities.”

Successive British governments have welcomed Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation between the two countries. About 150,000 Chinese students currently study at UK universities, contributing £7bn to the UK economy every year. Concerns have been growing in recent years, however, about the potential risks of such close collaboration.

On 30 September, MI5 warned vice-chancellors that a Chinese state-owned conglomerate called the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) had funded 100 or more academics in return for access to research which found its way back to China’s intelligence service.

The claim was denied by the Chinese embassy. Before that there was outcry when it emerged Sheffield Hallam University had complied with a demand from Beijing to halt research about human rights abuses in China .

Condemning the trip to China, the shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said Powell’s priorities were all wrong. “Instead of seeking closer ties to China, Powell should clamp down on CCP [Chinese Communist party] attempts to influence our own universities & its treatment of those who criticise it,” she posted on X.

Luke de Pulford, the executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, wrote on X: “Mind-blowingly shortsighted in policy terms.”

“What might seem to the uninitiated like an economic opportunity, or short-term hope to plug a gap in finances may actually be the government signing UK high education’s death warrant.

“If the balance tips too far towards dependence; if Beijing gets enough leverage, these institutions will cease to operate freely, and continue to leak IP and sensitive research to an adversary.”

after newsletter promotion

Sam Dunning, the director of UK-China Transparency, said the UK was in unprecedented territory. “British universities have never been so financially dependent on foreign students as they are today on Chinese students,” he said.

“Nor have there ever been more foreign nationals from any one country than British nationals studying Stem at an elite level in our top institutions, as is the case with China today.

“We are in unprecedented territory and on perilous terrain. The public interest demands careful, long-term thinking about these issues, and not continued short-termism.”

The summit forms part of government plans to grow education exports to £40bn a year by 2030. “British education is one of our country’s greatest strengths,” said Powell. “Expanding that internationally is a massive opportunity for our economy and wider society.

“Education builds lasting relationships and creates opportunities, but it also gives us the relationships and channels we need to have open and honest conversations. That is why we are putting education at the heart of clear-eyed engagement with China, using Britain’s world-class reputation to support growth, strengthen our global standing and stand up for what matters to Britain.”

stories.title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
stories.summary: Claire Waxman tells the BBC Andy Burnham needs to put justice in his 10-year plan for government.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Claire Waxman said the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe

Published 24 November 2026, 06:02 GMT

The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government.

Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month.

She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward.

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

'Very poor' letters

Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees".

Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme , the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives.

Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early.

She said she was "still waiting to see" data about the impact of releases on the ground, adding it had been around a year since the last meeting of the National Criminal Justice Board, an oversight body for the justice system.

'Broken system'

As part of the latest survey, the commissioner is recommending that all crime victims should receive a victim identifier number to track their progress through the criminal justice system.

The survey report will argue this would improve coordination between different agencies, as well as allowing victims to monitor when they will access the various legal rights they have under the Victims' Code.

It will also call for an "end-to-end" review of how victims navigate the system, similar to recent reviews that have focused on sentencing or the courts.

Responding to the survey results, Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones said the government was doing "everything we can to fix the broken system we inherited".

She added that ministers had already taken steps to improve the court backlog, and would be publishing an update to the Victims' Code next year.

She said this would be easier for victims to understand, and would set "clear expectations for criminal justice agencies and help victims feel supported".

stories.title: No 10 North will face greater scrutiny as Burnham's 10-year plan looms
stories.summary: The work of Number 10 North in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026, 00:31 GMT

The work of Andy Burnham's new Number 10 North office in Manchester has been kept largely away from the headlines since it opened in July.

But the officials based there are mainly focused on two soon-to-be-published documents that could go on to define his time as prime minister.

The first is Burnham's 10-year plan, which is due next month, and which the prime minister says will lay out a path "to where I believe we all want Britain to be".

The second is the 'rewiring the state' white paper, a detailed policy document that will follow in the new year and should give the clearest indication yet of what power Burnham hopes to move away from Westminster to other parts of the country.

But despite Burnham insisting his new Manchester team will be the "engine room" of change, others in government question how much difference they can really make.

There's talk among Labour MPs that the 10-year plan, which has also had significant input from Westminster departments, will not go as far as the prime minister had hoped.

But one official who has seen elements of the plan said it will be "pretty weighty" and include "quite a lot of radicalism".

Number 10 North has been focused on how the plan can deliver on Burnham's pledge to achieve "growth in every postcode".

One major theme is expected to be reindustrialisation, with advisers exploring how to attract businesses to less prosperous towns and cities.

Staff in Manchester are also said to be looking at what parts of the country may not see growth through reindustrialisation – such as some rural and coastal areas – and what the alternative offer for those places could be.

Eyebrows were raised in Whitehall this summer when a government statement said that "local economic growth policy" would be transferred "from HM Treasury directly into No 10 North".

Some saw that as an attempt to disempower the Treasury, but sources there insist that no serious decisions on growth can be made without the department's involvement and approval.

Burnham's Number 10 North goes on multi-million pound hiring spree Published 30 October

'Mindset shift' needed within government on No10 North, says deputy Published 21 October

When Burnham first announced plans for the Manchester base, he singled out housing as an issue on which it would take the lead.

In a speech last month Number 10 North's deputy director highlighted health, transport and education as other areas it was focused on.

While it's understood the 10-year plan is likely to include long-term ambitions for social care, skills training and council housebuilding, there are doubts within government departments about exactly how involved Number 10 North will eventually be in those areas.

One Whitehall official said "most things" that have been announced as Number 10 North priorities have in practice "stayed with other departments".

They said Number 10 North is "not doing delivery" because it "doesn't have its own resource" and is "underpowered compared to departments" in London.

A recent hiring spree will see around 120 officials and advisers working from Number 10 North when it moves into its permanent premises next spring.

That is almost half of the around 280 staff members that work for "Number 10 South", a term some advisers are now using for Downing Street.

But even those staffing levels are only a fraction of the numbers employed by other departments.

The Treasury's north of England campus in Darlington, which was set up in 2021, has around 3,000 staff.

John Healey is said to have been particularly impressed with the Darlington campus's record of hiring people who would otherwise not have joined the civil service, something Downing Street hopes to achieve in Manchester too.

Darlington's most senior civil servant, Beth Russell, has been working with Number 10 North to share her experience of how best to set up a new government office outside London.

Prime ministers have for decades been frustrated by how little power Number 10 can sometimes wield within Whitehall, arguing that levers can be pulled but nothing then happens.

One question at the heart of the Number 10 North project is whether it will eventually wield genuine power itself or merely decide which powers to take from Westminster and give to mayors and other regional politicians around the country.

A government source said Number 10 North's current role is "more in convening" people from elsewhere and argued the prime minister would need to choose what he wanted it to do in the future.

They added: "I could see it going two different ways.

"Will it be more delivery or will it be more in the conventional role of Number 10?

"Maybe it's not best placed to do things, but maybe directing and convening are also important things to do."

In July Burnham chaired the first meeting of the National Economic Council at No 10 North, bringing together ministers and regional mayors

Regional mayors have been regular visitors of Number 10 North and are set to be earmarked for much more expansive powers in the 'rewiring the state' white paper.

England currently has 14 metro mayors, a number which is likely to be expanded in the coming years.

Sources in both Number 10 and the Treasury say "fiscal devolution" will be a major part of the Burnham agenda.

People close to the prime minister say that is likely to ultimately mean more cash-raising, spending and borrowing power for mayors.

Two of Burnham's early announcements this summer saw mayors given a share of income tax and the ability to introduce a tourist tax for people visiting their areas.

The Treasury believes one of the most underreported elements of Healey's Budget last month was a £1.5bn borrowing facility that will be given to mayors from 2028.

Sources say that in the future projects such as Doncaster-Sheffield Airport, which Healey gave his backing to, could be given the financial go-ahead directly by mayors, without the need for a separate thumbs up from the chancellor.

For now mayors have each been asked to submit a list of projects to Number 10 North, which they feel are being held up by government processes.

Government departments in Westminster have also been asked to identify what areas they are currently responsible for which could potentially be devolved to mayors and other local government officials.

What's less clear is how the prime minister's devolution plans will affect Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and whether he is keen for them too to adopt a mayoral model.

At a recent meeting in Glasgow, Burnham said he would discuss that further with the leaders of the devolved nations.

He recently rejected a proposal from the First Minister of Wales to devolve more responsibilities over policing and justice.

Away from the gaze of backbench MPs, opposition parties and Westminster journalists, Number 10 North has so far been able to go about its business without drawing much attention.

But as Burnham's long-term plans for the country start to become more clear, the scrutiny faced by his Manchester power base is likely to grow too.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?
stories.summary: The BBC's Chris Mason analyses what the EU conversation means for Labour and the PM.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026, 00:45 GMT

When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader , promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham Published 22 hours ago

He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."

Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?

Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.

A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.

And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.

It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.

Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?

Ursula von der Leyen, Andy Burnham and António Costa at the EU-UK Summit in Brussels last week.

Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."

They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.

On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over.

How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.

Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.

But even if all these things are agreed – and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas – Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.

It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

stories.summary: The first minister asks for an urgent meeting after Andy Burnham rejected calls for more powers in Cardiff.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham says he is "not persuaded" by the case for more powers

Published 23 November 2026

The first minister says he wants an urgent meeting with the prime minister after Andy Burnham rejected calls to give more powers to the Welsh government.

Rhun ap Iorwerth said he was "deeply disappointed" and that Burnham "does not view Wales as an equal nation".

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates urged Burnham to "negotiate around a table" with ap Iorwerth.

In a letter to ap Iorwerth last week, the prime minister said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve policing and justice , the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the UK government believed "devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another".

Trade union body TUC Cymru said it was disappointing calls for further devolution had been "dismissed without any discussion".

In a written statement to Senedd members, the first minister said: "The refusal to even explore the devolution of the crown estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation.

"The case in favour of Wales having control over these areas of responsibility - just like Scotland - is compelling. Several commissions have argued for the devolution of justice and policing, yet the UK government seemingly prefers to put unionist ideology before hard evidence.

"This government is not interested in more powers for power's sake. The current settlement is unfair, unjust and unsustainable."

Rhun ap Iorwerth is Plaid Cymru leader and first minister of Wales

In a letter to the prime minister, ap Iorwerth asked the prime minister to reconsider the work of previous reports on the issue.

He said he would "welcome an urgent meeting with you to discuss the evidence and agree a substantive way forward".

Meanwhile, Skates called on the Welsh and UK governments to continue talks on the devolution of powers.

He called for "greater detail" on why further devolution of policing was not happening, and said he will be meeting with Burnham himself.

Welsh Labour has not dropped calls for the devolution of justice, the Crown Estate and rail investment.

"You negotiate around a table," he said. "And you don't walk away when work needs to continue. Devolution is a process, not an event and Welsh Labour's position remains clear that we support further devolution to and within Wales."

Skates continued: "Devolution of employment support is vital in getting to grips with the crisis of youth unemployment. The devolution of innovation funding will help strengthen the economy.

"Devolution of youth justice will lead to better integration of youth services and social services and the justice system.

"We need action as fast as possible in bringing these powers to Wales and in ensuring they go to the right people and places.

"On policing, progress is being made, but I want greater detail over why full devolution is not happening as part of the current reforms."

Meanwhile, TUC Cymru's general secretary, Laura Doel, said: "Our focus is on securing the powers and resources needed to improve outcomes for working people. That must include fair funding for Wales.

"These are the long-established views of TUC Cymru and it's disappointing that our calls have been dismissed without any discussion.

"We ask that the UK government does more to respect and engage with the democratic institutions in Wales and listens to the voice of Welsh workers, rather than closing down proposals for further devolution before they have been properly considered."

Kinnock said: "The prime minister's offer reflects our view that devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another and that he instead wants each government to consider, alongside local authority partners, how we can empower Welsh regions to use both reserved and devolved powers to drive economic growth.

"What matters is what works."

stories.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
stories.summary: The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Army said on Sunday that it would carry out the detonation on Wednesday.

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

Late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and plans.

Lead azide risk

Documents released by the Army last week said that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

In late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a New York Times report . MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

But two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s plans, the Times reported. The company’s founder said MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response.

Now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and that it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion. Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

Imminent threat

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend . “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”

The Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

Last Thursday, Telle said that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday .

In his social media post Monday, Trump said he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.

In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contract was canceled.

“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.

stories.body:
John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, the US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang ’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, by which the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union , the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders were either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

stories.title: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham
stories.summary: The prime minister also said his predecessors who have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate are "stuck in the past".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Burnham made the comments while addressing MPs in parliament on Monday

Published 23 November 2026

The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to MPs.

Andy Burnham told the Commons there was "no fixed destination" on talks to explore closer ties with the European Union, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

After several former prime ministers urged him to not reopen the Brexit debate, Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" - and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

At a summit on Friday, Burnham agreed a new deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

He also finalised the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU and said both sides will "brainstorm" options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Conservative MP Sir Edward Leigh said the "reset" with the EU is "a prelude to the prime minister's sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum" and risked leading to another Scottish independence referendum.

Burnham replied to the Gainsborough MP: "It's not a prelude to anything. It's a pragmatic approach and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't. There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination.

"Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we'll have to obviously watch how life changes. But where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress."

'No banging on about Europe'

The prime minister also told MPs the government's forthcoming 10-year plan for the country will consider the "range of options for our long-term relationship with our largest market" - the EU.

MPs heard the "plan for Britain" will be published next month and the results of the "informal exchanges of ideas" with the EU will be presented around the time of their next joint summit.

To laughter from the opposition benches, Burnham said: "So there will be no banging on about Europe from this side or a running commentary."

The words echoed those used by Conservative former Prime Minister Lord Cameron in 2006 .

Burnham went on to say there would be a "calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interests in the long-term", adding "always the British people will be the boss and they will decide what comes next".

Conservative MP Sir Bernard Jenkin asked Burnham to "give a clear and unequivocal statement that it would be unthinkable for any prime minister to try and take the UK back into the EU without a referendum".

Burnham replied to the Harwich and North Essex MP : "Yes, it would be unthinkable."

Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done' Published 2 days ago

'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen? Published 2 days ago

Speaking for the Opposition, Badenoch said Burnham's EU deal "wasn't really about reducing the cost of living" but instead "committing Britain to becoming a rule taker from Brussels, something he had no mandate to do".

Badenoch also said: "Six former prime ministers, including Tony Blair, are criticising the direction he is taking UK-EU relations. He says the prime ministers who implemented a democratic decision are living in the past.

"The only person living in the past is the man trying to take Britain back to 2015 instead of focusing on the future."

Over the weekend, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, told the BBC she was "aghast" Burnham could be considering rejoining.

She urged him to "accept Brexit and move on".

Rishi Sunak has also warned against reopening the "divisive" debate about rejoining the EU, telling Sky News it would be "a huge distraction for government".

Earlier this month, Boris Johnson, who negotiated the original Brexit deal as prime minister, said it was "madness" for Burnham to make Brexit his "political priority".

He told the Daily Telegraph , external , he believed the public would back Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

His predecessor Lord Cameron, who resigned as prime minister after losing the 2016 Brexit referendum, has also warned against "another-decade long debate about whether we should be in or out".

Meanwhile, former Labour Prime Minister Sir Tony - who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU - has said the UK should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

Asked about the criticism from his predecessors, Burnham earlier told broadcasters: "They're stuck in the past because they can't face up to the bad deal that they did."

He added: "I'm not a prime minister that's going to be stuck in the past."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed the new agreements before telling the Commons that a "totally new deal for Britain" is needed now.

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice labelled it a "terrible" deal, while Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said "bold and brave politics, not baby steps" are needed.

stories.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
stories.summary: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang "did nothing wrong."
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.”

Originally published November 23, 2026

Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals .

The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures.

Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

“We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.”

We’ll be right back after this brief interruption

Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak.

Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement.

Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back.

In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation.

In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer.

This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.
